messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Rajan, a 64-year-old South Asian man and warehouse worker, has been struggling with the aftermath of his captivity experience for several months now. Married and otherwise content in his personal life, he finds himself increasingly entangled in a cycle of fear and avoidance that is disrupting his daily routine and causing significant distress. Mr. Rajan’s trauma began when he was held captive by individuals who kept him locked up during night-time hours, using threats and intimidation to maintain control over him. The traumatic event occurred at 3 AM, a time that has since become profoundly disturbing for him. He recalls the dark, confined space and the constant fear of being alone with his captors in the darkness. The sound of snakes, which he saw as metaphors for danger and unpredictability during his captivity, also became deeply unsettling. In the weeks following his release, Mr. Rajan started to avoid going to sleep or lying in the dark due to his intense fear that it would bring back memories of his ordeal. Night-time or waking up in the dark now triggers a cascade of distressing thoughts and feelings. This aversion to darkness leads him to constantly check for signs of danger around him, even when he is at home, where there are no real threats. His wife often finds him pacing the house at night, unable to settle down. When she asks what’s wrong, he admits to her that he can’t stop thinking about being captured again and feels a deep sense of helplessness. Mr. Rajan also seeks reassurance frequently from his family members, asking them repeatedly if they think it is safe for him to be alone at night or if they believe he can handle the memories of captivity. This constant need for validation has strained their relationship; however, Mr. Rajan feels that without this reassurance, he would spiral into a state of panic and dread. Mr. Rajan’s fears are exacerbated by his hypervigilance throughout the day. He is superalert or watchful, often looking behind him to check if someone is following him. The time around 3 AM triggers intense anxiety for him, making it nearly impossible to feel safe at night. These feelings of heightened threat contribute to his belief that he cannot prevent bad things from happening again, further reinforcing his sense of helplessness. His negative appraisals also fuel the cycle of fear and avoidance. Mr. Rajan is certain that if he thinks about the event, he will not be able to handle it. This thought avoidance has led him to become increasingly isolated, as even small reminders like photos or discussions about snakes can trigger his anxiety. He now avoids many activities and places where such triggers might appear. As a warehouse worker, Mr. Rajan’s workplace environment is particularly challenging. The dark corners of the warehouse and occasional nighttime shifts have become overwhelming for him. He has started to miss work more frequently, partly due to his inability to sleep well at night and partly because he fears being alone in the building after hours. His coworkers notice that he is constantly checking behind him, even while working, which has affected his job performance. Mr. Rajan finally decided to seek help when he realized how much his condition was affecting not just his life but also those around him. He is most afraid of losing control and being unable to protect himself or his family again. Despite the overwhelming fear, Mr. Rajan hopes that with support, he can find a way to manage these distressing thoughts and regain some sense of normalcy in his daily life. The intertwined cycle of triggers, maladaptive strategies, threat perception, and negative appraisals has become a central part of Mr. Rajan’s experience, shaping nearly every aspect of his daily routine and interactions. He is now at the point where he recognizes that seeking professional help is crucial to breaking this cycle and reclaiming control over his life.
